title: Regarding AI... I need to get something off my chest publicly
author: Heavy_Extent_3863
selftext:
My last take on AI games for a while:

If everyone saying 'LOOK WHAT I DID WITH ONE PROMPT!' put that passion into a real game idea, spent time developing it, and put effort into the graphics, UI, story, and especially gameplay (!!!), we'd all be COOKED.

The truth is though, they're all just sloppy AI-slop kids... lazy fucks with no true motivation, passion, or talent for anything in life.

So, don't worry.

Use AI as a tool to bring your creativity, vision, and ideas to life, to break down barriers like budget, lack of specific skills, or the absence of a sounding board (not everyone has friends, family, or mentors). But for fuck's sake, don't take shortcuts. Don't be lazy. Don't settle for 'good enough' gameplay. Put the time in. The passion. The pain. Put every ounce of humanity you've got into it. Even with AI.

Try to take the harder route. Learn to code, even just a little bit. Learn to create sounds and music by yourself. Draw your Steam capsule art, just for the sake of feeling what it's like, and to better understand what all these elements actually take. With that knowledge, you'll know how to use AI in a proper way.

Or, you might just stick to one or two of those skills, backed by a true understanding of the difference between AI-slop and real art.

...  
Sorry, just needed to get that off my chest as a bit of self-therapy. I'm working on a game full-time, doing everything myself: pixel art, music, audio. Thousands of hours put in. Programming is the one thing I can't do without AI. I'm a terrible coder. Rooting for all of us! おやすみ

It was gonna be a running joke in the series, but once I posted, people said they didnt continue watching and wished me to fail cause i used an AI asset. My friend is a professional gambler so its a bit weird but that whole group thinks of themselves as artists and write music/books as a semi hobby so I can understand the pain point.  Either way its gonna be a wild couple of years for everyone and I couldn't hide it if I wanted to because I pivoted at work to being the 'ai expert' and got it added to my title for my last promotion. Thankfully my siblings are also excelling so no family problems - my sister who I helped get good with it is saving her company millions of dollars a year just making skills and my brother is a engineering VP and they've gone all in but for people who can't pivot.

comments.author: VibeForTokens
comments.body:
I personally have 0 issues with the "one prompt" posts and YouTube videos. The recent changes with Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, finally got to a useful state that I created a PoC stage for a game I wanted to make. So I did the PRD with Opus and told Sonnet to make it happen. I had it created in Three.js cause I wanted to give it the best chance at a one-shot. 

It got it close enough where I could test out if the idea in my brain was as fun as I thought it might be. I enjoyed it enough that I converted that game to Godot so that I can release it on the App Stores and Steam, if it does well enough on mobile. Now I'm going through and play testing / fixing it until I feel it's "good enough" to release. Probably take another Month+, but it's been going well. 

All that to say one-shot prompts are great for testing out an idea before getting serious about it. I'm not interested in a 5yr passion project.

comments.author: UnmarkedWestDev
comments.body:
Agree with every word, especially the part about learning a bit of everything.

I’m old enough to have written assembly on 8-bit machines, back when my first games came out in the 80s. There was no other way then: you built your own tools, and if nobody else could do the sound, you did it. Nobody called it “taking the harder route”. It was the only route, and it taught you what every piece of a game costs.

Today I’m making a game in C++ on my own engine, and after my initial architectural set up, AI writes most of the code. I've made games for 35 years, it's time to rest, I don't give a fuck about people calling me lazy. It’s the biggest productivity jump I’ve seen in my career, bigger than going from assembly to C and C++ and graphical tools and visual debuggers etc. But it changed the cost of execution, not the hard part (in making games). The AI gives you the median of everything it has seen: clean, working, and the same as what everyone else gets. You need to steer the AI and you need to have deep knowledge of the game development process to obtain results that are meaningful. That's why 100% of zero-shot prompted games are total slop. Garbage in, garbage out, this rule always applies.

replies.author: broncos4thewin
replies.body: See I have tried to make games before but always got caught up with the art side. Now Claude code can make me retro pixel art (I’m old school too and those are the games I want to make) it’s like the floodgates opening. But is the art bit kinda cheating a bit more than coding? As a musician and filmmaker by background it feels like it is, but maybe it shouldn’t? The game I’m working on is the opposite of one-shot slop, it’s taking me weeks of back and forth with Claude code (it’s a retro point and click set in the 80s as it happens, slasher genre) but I know the game dev community would still hate the shortcuts.

replies.author: UnmarkedWestDev
replies.body:
It’s not cheating, but it can certainly be unethical. The real question is: would you have the money to pay a human artist? If not, it’s not greed, it’s lack of alternatives. Though to be fair, working with Claude is a lot easier than working with a human being...

But are you really sure the result is good? Most of what I see made with AI honestly isn’t. There are inconsistencies everywhere, no artistic coherence, and every screen is in a slightly different style. As a musician you’d spot an AI track that’s off in two seconds. Judge your pixel art the same way.

The anti-AI factions will want to burn you regardless, but most players don’t care. Big studios already use AI in production, on mobile even more, and nobody cares because nobody knows. If your game holds up, don’t worry about the haters. An 80s slasher point and click sounds like a good idea, by the way.

comments.author: Ganiam
comments.body:
You can get really great projects done solely with Ai, but most are looking for something fast and it turns out sloppy. I’ve seen very few games out here that look “fun” at all. People get working prototype and that’s great and all, but very little of what I’ve seen about their sprites moving around seems fun to play at all.

I think whenever we get new tools like this, people rush to produce something just to have a product but they miss out on a lot. Reminds me of shovelware games from the 90’s or 2000’s. Stuff kids would make fun of each other for owning.

But buried behind all the crap there are some genuinely passionate people who are producing genuinely interesting looking games using only AI. But those are very few and fewer are ready to launch because even with AI, game development takes a lot of time

comments.author: bionic-brawl-online
comments.body: Really, you can use AI as a model, too. "AI, program this feature. Include comments to explain which parts of the code are doing what." Then go through, read the code, and try to make sense of what the AI did. Change a few things, see what happens. Really try to understand how it works, and then look for ways to improve it- because AI is not an efficient coding machine! It'll get the job done, typically, but.. yeah. There are places to polish it up.

comments.author: Ruan_XMKGames
comments.body: I can vouch for this... i decided to become a developer because i love the craft... i would ABSOLUTLY LOVE doing this full time from home... yes i only have a masters in JAVA... so i started with unity, i do use AI as tools for help but not building a full game with one promt... my 1st game Ascendustry is now live on google play released a couple of days ago... took me 7 months to build working late nights and after hours after my full time day job and spending time with my wife and baby boy...but i had to start doing somthing extra... so i started...stumbled...learned...debugged HOURS apon end...and finaly...got live... and sure i still have ALOT of work still needs to be done...and there is ALWAYS room for improvements! i take PRIDE in my work...and Yes im not a super proffesional studio with sponsors and capital...i work on a shitty rig that i hope to god lasts till i can afford a new one... building an aab of 180mb takes an hour...cpu burning at a 100% during that time... so yes A.I made this possible for me... to help provide better for my family while working from home.... but the invention...the strategies.. the building...changing from hard code to fully data driven systems i all learned the HARD way... and surely enough my 2nd game is heading to closed testing soon...and went ALOT better because of what i learned making Ascendustry...to ALL the others out there...take pride in your work please...there is NO way as an easy way...HARD WORK, DEDICATION, ALOT OF TIME and headaches makes the end result somthing you can honestly brag about and say...I created this....Peace out fellow Devs!
